name: Digitaria

project_scope.note: Only the two installed taxa, not a complete county Digitaria flora. D. ciliaris introduced; D. cognata native to Texas, but native-by-county audit not performed or changed.

look_here_first: DIGITARIA — two installed Central Texas study plants look very different. Southern crabgrass (D. ciliaris) has compact clustered fingerlike one-sided RACEMES, with overlapping/paired spikelets along a branch; fall witchgrass (D. cognata, formerly Leptoloma cognatum) has an airy widely forked PANICLE with tiny separated oval spikelets at threadlike tips. Confirm using the same-plant base, ligule, and a measured ripe spikelet. One flowering silhouette is an entry clue, never full species proof.

recognition.where_to_look_first: Open both genuine photo galleries. Find a fingerlike raceme cluster versus the airy, delicate branched broom. Then zoom on the attached reproductive units, not general foliage color.
priority: Entire flowering HEAD architecture, including attachment pattern of racemes/panicle branches
Dense ONE-SIDED overlapping spikelets on raceme vs separated terminal units on wiry panicle
Mature intact paired spikelets on winged crabgrass raceme vs individual oval fall-witchgrass spikelets
Rooted annual/decumbent ciliaris nodes vs perennial basal fall-witchgrass tuft
True membranous ciliaris ligule; fall-witchgrass branch axil hairs and asymmetrically waved blade edge
Measure glume/lemma parts for similar other crabgrasses, especially D. sanguinalis
recognition.photo_guardrail: No photo here verifies upper/lower glume vein counts, ciliaris two attached pedicels, cognata radiating hairy branch nodes, a wavy leaf margin, a true ligule or native Hays County occurrence. Annotate only visible structures.

comparison_lesson.memory_rule: FINGERS + PACKED SPIKELETS = SOUTHERN CRABGRASS. AIRY WIRY BROOM + ISOLATED OVAL SPIKELETS = FALL WITCHGRASS.
quick_split: SOUTHERN CRABGRASS: first look for several clustered, mostly fingerlike one-sided flowering RACEMES with tightly overlapping spikelets in pairs along each flattened branch, not an airy broom. The original photo is ONLY a spikelet exterior; use the two new credited real photos for whole raceme layout and dry overlapping spikelets. A spreading usually annual plant may root at low nodes. Confirm the membranous ligule (~1–3 mm), ripe ~2.5–3.5 mm paired spikelets and sterile lower-lemma vein ornamentation under magnification before separating similar D. sanguinalis.

FALL WITCHGRASS (formerly Leptoloma cognatum): look for an extremely OPEN, diffuse broomlike panicle on hair-fine wiry stems with solitary small oval spikelets near branch ends. Three real source photographs now show the head, basal leafy tuft, and isolated terminal spikelets. The characteristic swollen pubescent branch junctions and pale crinkled blade margin still need actual macro pictures; don't draw these hairs on unresolvable pixels. Native to Texas at STATE scale, but Hays BONAP county status remains unchanged/unverified.
closeouts: D. ciliaris may root at decumbent nodes, but root development is not shown by its three photo panels. Collect/legal photograph the actual same-plant base.
D. cognata (Leptoloma cognatum in old references) is a perennial. Its Pennsylvania tuft photo shows basal leaves but cannot establish root persistence from a single season.
The tiny crabgrass spikelet close photo is NOT a whole-head picture; the added CC0 group-of-racemes picture teaches that role, and the CC BY close raceme teaches dense one-sided alignment.
D. sanguinalis and D. ischaemum need actual sterile-lemma nerve/prickle and measured spikelet comparisons. Erect vs creeping or simple hairiness is not enough.
BONAP/NAPA county certification remains untouched; existing introduced/native labels are not revised. Confirm Hays nativity separately before restoration metrics.
Other Digitaria taxa also occur in Texas. This is a two-species learner key, not an exhaustive county checklist.

visual_status: FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS: two installed Digitaria species, six source-reviewed licensed photo panels and sixteen visible-only arrows. Species cards and genus visual comparisons improved; missing legal rooted base, measured paired spikelet attachments, true ligule, cognata swollen hairy branch junction/wavy leaf margin and ciliaris vs sanguinalis sterile-lemma vein macro.
visual_needs: D. ciliaris same-plant whole head PLUS legal rooted spreading lower stems/actual nodes, with scale
D. ciliaris paired unequal spikelet pedicels on winged rachis under 10–20×
D. ciliaris membranous 1–3 mm ligule and ciliaris versus sanguinalis matched ripe sterile lemma dorsal nerves
D. cognata swollen hairy branch axils truly visible with 1-mm scale
D. cognata one leaf showing a wavy pale margin opposite straighter edge and separate rooted perennial base
Same-scale mature glume and floret view for both species with voucher determination
what_to_teach_crew: START at the two original source-labelled photos, but note the ciliaris original is a spikelet close-up; the visible wild flowering-head silhouette is shown by a separate CC0 source.
Have crew match an actual flowering head to near-parallel one-sided racemes with packed spikelets OR a fragile, airy, forked panicle with widely separated oval spikelets.
Document a root base and leaf collar on the SAME specimen. Fingerlike crabgrass usually annual, native fall witchgrass perennial; these cannot be proven with loose head photos.
For ciliaris: sample an intact mature raceme, verify TWO spikelets at branch node with unequal stalk lengths, winged rachis and true membranous ligule.
For cognata: photograph the actual swollen hairy branch junction and opposite pale/undulating blade margin under scale; existing whole-head photos lack microscopic proof.
When confused with large/smooth crabgrass, measure sterile lower lemma veins and glume ratios at 10–20×; 'looks hairy' is not enough.
Cognata synonym Leptoloma cognatum must not generate a duplicate card; county native metrics are not inferred from this field teaching lesson.
